title: TOAST Storage & MVCC Internals
description: Deep dive into PostgreSQL page architecture (8KB pages), TOAST out-of-line compression, xmin/xmax tuple headers, and visibility maps.

data.text: PostgreSQL stores table data in fixed-size **8KB disk pages**. Because a physical row tuple cannot span across multiple pages, how does PostgreSQL store large values like a 10MB text article or a 50MB PDF? The answer is **TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique)**.
How TOAST Works Under the Hood

When a row exceeds ~2KB (one-fourth of an 8KB page), the TOAST engine first attempts to compress large columns using `pglz` or `lz4`. If still too large, it moves the column data out of the main heap table into a separate secondary TOAST table, leaving only an 18-byte pointer in the main row tuple.

rows: The transaction ID that inserted this tuple. A transaction can only see this row if `xmin` has committed.
The transaction ID that deleted or updated this tuple. Once committed, transactions starting afterward consider this row invisible.

data.text: Ctrl-C, Dirty Pages, and Atomic Writes

Two safety mechanisms sit underneath MVCC. The Write-Ahead Log records every change before the page is written to disk, so after a crash PostgreSQL can replay committed changes and discard uncommitted ones. A full-page write after each checkpoint protects against torn pages caused by a crash mid-write on an 8KB page.

data.title: Inspecting WAL settings and crash recovery
data.content: `full_page_writes` is on by default and should stay on unless the filesystem guarantees atomic 8KB writes. `wal_level` controls how much information is written, which affects replication and logical decoding.

data.title: Interview angle: durability is a trade-off you choose
data.text: `synchronous_commit = off` lets a transaction return before its WAL is flushed, which speeds up writes at the cost of possibly losing the last few milliseconds of committed transactions if the server crashes. It never corrupts the database, because WAL replay still leaves a consistent state. Being able to separate durability (losing recent commits) from consistency (database corruption) is a precise and impressive answer.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: TOAST transparently compresses and splits large columns into secondary storage.
Reading a table without requesting TOAST columns avoids reading TOAST tables entirely.
`xmin` and `xmax` embedded in every tuple header power PostgreSQL's lock-free MVCC snapshots.
